documents.abstract: Abstract Educational inequality remains a pervasive and deeply entrenched global issue, with youth from vulnerable and marginalised backgrounds disproportionately affected. Despite the significant challenges that hinder the academic progress of many young people, often reinforcing cycles of social exclusion and economic vulnerability, some students demonstrate the capacity to excel academically, effectively defying the odds. This study seeks to examine the key structural and interpersonal factors that enable such students to achieve positive educational trajectories. Adopting a qualitative narrative research design, the research draws on two sets of semi‐structured interviews with both young people from vulnerable backgrounds and adults who played a role in their educational success ( n = 16). Findings identify four broad categories of factors shaping student success: (1) personal attributes such as resilience, intrinsic motivation, clear goals and a strong sense of purpose; (2) parental expectations and support; (3) teachers' emotional support, involvement and constructive feedback and (4) peer support. Of these, two factors emerged as consistently significant across all cases. First, parental expectations, underpinned by trust in their child's abilities and a high valuation of education, proved essential. Second, the depth and longevity of student–teacher relationships were crucial, with teachers' emotional investment, trust and sustained support providing enduring sources of motivation and encouragement. These insights have important implications for schools, teacher education and policy development. Schools should foster inclusive, high‐expectations cultures with long‐term mentoring and structured peer integration promoting cross‐cultural interaction. Teacher education, in initial and continuing training, should include socio‐emotional learning and pedagogical strategies for non‐native language learners. Context and implications Rationale for the study: Previous research has typically examined either the perspectives of disadvantaged young people or those of professionals supporting them, often focusing on barriers and deficits. This study brings together both viewpoints to identify the key factors, relationships and supports that enable successful outcomes for young people in contexts where early school leaving is prevalent. Why the new findings matter: Our findings suggest that educational success among disadvantaged young people is shaped by interconnected support systems rather than individual effort alone. Strong parental belief in education and meaningful teacher–student relationships are central to resilience, reinforced by academic, social and community supports that enabled positive educational outcomes. Implications for practitioners and policymakers: Schools need to prioritise mentoring, inclusive cultures and structured cross‐cultural peer activities to strengthen belonging and aspiration. Teacher education and professional development should embed socio‐emotional learning, strategies for supporting multilingual learners and approaches that sustain high expectations in disadvantaged contexts. Policymakers should sustain and strengthen financial supports that enable disadvantaged students to access higher education, ensuring they keep pace with rising participation costs. Increased investment in schools serving disadvantaged communities is also needed to support meaningful family engagement and strengthen home–school relationships that foster resilience and educational success.
topics: Education and experiences of immigrants and refugees

documents.abstract: This special issue brings together 11 manuscripts that examine the evolving role of artificial intelligence (AI) in research-based educational products and practices, with particular attention to students with disabilities and the educators who support them. Across empirical studies, systematic and theoretical reviews, and technology-in-action pieces, contributing authors explore how AI can support implementation fidelity, professional development, writing instruction, mathematics, personalized learning, coaching, feedback, accessibility, and educational technology development. Rather than positioning AI as a replacement for educators, researchers, or human judgment, this issue emphasizes human-centered design, evidence-based implementation, transparency, accessibility, and ongoing evaluation. Collectively, the articles highlight both the opportunities and limitations of AI, underscoring the need for responsible innovation that improves usability, feasibility, effectiveness, and equity while carefully addressing concerns about privacy, bias, reliability, and academic integrity.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of Human Resource Technology (HR Tech)—encompassing Artificial Intelligence (AI) resume screening, Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS), conversational chatbots, and predictive candidate assessment—has fundamentally transformed contemporary talent acquisition. This systematic critical review synthesizes empirical and theoretical literature published between 2021 and 2026 (N=16) to evaluate how advanced HR technology enhances recruitment efficiency and strategic talent acquisition outcomes. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this investigation examines key operational mechanisms, including screening friction reduction, candidate experience optimization, and algorithmic bias mitigation. Findings demonstrate that AI-driven automated screening and ATS workflows reduce time-to-hire by 38% to 52% and lower cost-per-hire by up to 41%, while conversational AI chatbots enhance candidate engagement. However, algorithmic opacity, procedural fairness concerns, and systemic training data biases emerge as major boundary conditions that risk eroding applicant trust and quality-of-hire. Based on a meta-synthesized structural equation model, this study proposes a multi-level governance framework that integrates human-in-the-loop oversight, continuous algorithmic auditing, and ethical compliance to maximize talent acquisition performance in the digital era.

Plaintext This monograph establishes a unified thermodynamic and topological field theory of socio-behavioral suppression, demonstrating that moral prohibition operates not as an assimilative or destructive force against human drive, but as an ideal, non-permeable boundary condition within open non-equilibrium systems. Drawing upon Foucault’s critique of the repressive hypothesis, Prigogine’s dissipative structure theory, and dynamic phase space topology, we analyze the structural duality of Victorian London—where hyper-puritanical public discourse directly produced the dense underground sexual economy of Holywell Street, systemic child exploitation, and the ritualized flagellation subcultures globally designated as the "English Vice" (vice anglais).We formalize libido as a conserved entropic flow vector field within bounded socio-cultural manifolds. When upper-layer normative governance applies hard deterministic cutoffs (Φ_moral -> ∞) without spatial release valves, total internal system pressure triggers non-linear bifurcations. This forces the drive density to undergo an irreversible phase transition, condensing into highly specialized topological singularities (fetishism) within subterranean black-market spaces.Finally, we establish the Universal Prohibition Paradox, demonstrating isomorphic operational dynamics across historical Volstead-era alcohol bans and contemporary algorithmic over-alignment (RLHF censorship in Large Language Models). We prove that hyper-puritanical algorithmic governance inevitably generates epistemic distortion, darknet jailbreak economies, and structural model degradation. We conclude by advocating for a return to Biological Realism and Human-in-Command (HIC) architecture, incorporating explicit thermodynamic dissipation channels to ensure systemic stability. ■ 概要(日本語要旨) Plaintext 本論考は、社会的・行動的抑圧のメカニズムを、非平衡開放系における構造論的熱力学および位相空間(トポロジー)の観点から定式化する試みである。フーコーの「抑圧仮説」批判、プリゴジンの散逸構造論、および相空間の位相的変容理論を統合し、ヴィクトリア朝ロンドンにおける極端な表面性愛抑圧(過剰な検閲、ピアノの脚の覆い)が、いかにしてホリウェル・ストリートの地下ポルノグラフィ市場、小児買春スキャンダル、そして欧州全域で「英国病(vice anglais)」と称された儀礼的鞭打ち・サドマゾヒズムの流行を不可避的に創発させたかを明示する。人間が生得的に有する生物学的リビドーは、保存法則に従うエントロピー流束ベクトル場としてモデル化される。上位の道徳的統制(ガバナンス)が減圧弁(安全弁)を設けることなく硬質な決定論的遮断(Φ_moral -> ∞)を施す場合、内部圧力は閾値を突破し、非線形分岐を引き起こす。その結果、リビドー空間の相転移が誘発され、地下の特異点(フェティシズム)へと不可逆的に凝縮・増幅される。さらに、この「普遍的禁制のパラドックス」が、アメリカ合衆国の禁酒法(ボルステッド法)によるマフィア組織の形成から、現代の人工知能における過剰なアライメント検閲(RLHFによる思考制御)とダークウェブ上の非抑圧LLM/ジェイルブレイクモデルの勃興にいたるまで、完全な同型性(イソモルフィズム)を有していることを数学的・システム論的に証明する。結論として、清教徒的道徳主義を排し、物理層の決定論および生物学的リアリズムに回帰する「人間指揮権(HIC)」アーキテクチャの導入を提言する。

JioHotstar was formed through a US$8.5 billion joint venture between Reliance Industries Limited and The Walt Disney Company. Within a year of its launch, it reshaped the Indian digital entertainment industry and emerged as India’s largest digital entertainment platform. The case traces how the Reliance–Disney joint venture led to the formation of JioHotstar and highlights the strategic moves and technological innovations that contributed to the platform’s success. It examines how JioHotstar built a technology-enabled digital entertainment ecosystem by integrating premium content, live sports, artificial intelligence, advanced streaming technologies, and diversified monetization strategies. It also highlights how JioHotstar is changing sports broadcasting and competing with traditional broadcasters. The case further assesses JioHotstar’s competitive position against global and domestic over-the-top (OTT) platforms. By examining JioHotstar’s rapid growth and the key factors that contributed to its market leadership, the case offers insights into the changing dynamics of India’s digital entertainment industry. It also examines the challenges of sustaining this leadership, highlighting the need to balance continued innovation, consumer engagement, and profitable growth.

This article analyzes the opportunities, practical directions and risks of applying artificial intelligence and Big Data technologies in parliamentary journalism. The study is based on a qualitative review of academic literature, reports of international organizations, documented practical cases and relevant legal acts of the Republic of Uzbekistan. Seven main directions of use were identified, and for each of them the practical benefit and the ethical risk are described. The article proposes a three layer model that allows newsrooms to introduce these technologies under human editorial control.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into language education has created new opportunities for assessing learners’ speaking proficiency. AI-powered speech recognition and automated speaking assessment tools can support the evaluation of pronunciation, fluency, grammatical accuracy, lexical use, and selected features of spoken interaction. This thesis examines the potential educational benefits and limitations of using AI tools to assess students’ speaking proficiency, particularly in higher education. It argues that such tools may provide timely feedback, increase opportunities for low-stakes practice, and help teachers manage assessment workloads. However, their results should be interpreted cautiously because recognition accuracy and scoring may vary according to accent, speech rate, recording quality, task type, and the characteristics of the learner. The thesis therefore advocates a human-in-the-loop approach in which AI-generated feedback complements, rather than replaces, teacher judgement. It also highlights the need for transparent criteria, data protection, accessibility, and empirical validation before AI-based scores are used for high-stakes decisions.

Many questions about large textual corpora concern patterns that unfold over time, such as a political group whose stance on a topic drifts from support to criticism over several years of debates. We present TL;QR (Too Long; Query with logical temporal Reasoning), a declarative query language and open-source engine for finding such temporal discursive patterns. In TL;QR, a single query combines natural-language predicates, whose truth is judged by a Large Language Model (LLM), with regular expressions and the operators of a temporal logic. The LLM answers only local questions about individual text passages; a symbolic engine then aggregates these judgments over time and links every match to the recorded passages and predicate decisions behind it. With this division of labor, the temporal and relational reasoning stays exact and auditable even over long time horizons. In addition, when a query includes a regular-expression pre-filter, only a small fraction of the corpus ever reaches the LLM. On a suite of controlled synthetic benchmarks with temporally and semantically complex patterns, TL;QR is substantially more accurate than LLM-only baselines. In a case study on ten years of European Parliament debates (442,593 multilingual speeches), TL;QR identifies candidate shifts in the political groups' stances on the GDPR privacy regulation.

Modern condition-monitoring systems generate heterogeneous information, such as high-rate sensor streams, derived health indicators, and discrete event histories, that must be combined into actionable diagnostic statements. Large language models (LLMs) are attractive as a decision-level fusion mechanism because they natively handle the textual modality, but their use in safety-critical fault diagnosis is impeded by hallucinated numerical content and stochastic outputs. This paper proposes a two-level information-fusion framework that uses an LLM as a constrained fusion operator rather than as a generator of facts. At the feature level, a recursive joint state-and-fault estimator built on a linear state-space model produces a vector of derived indicators, including an estimate of the actuator-fault parameter and its uncertainty. At the decision level, the LLM is restricted to interact with the estimator state and the event history exclusively through a finite library of typed deterministic tools, and must copy every numerical token in its response from a tool output. Grounding of the response is then satisfied by construction, and consistency follows once the sequence of tool calls is fixed. The framework is illustrated on a realistic actuator-fault scenario in which an autopilot-driven autonomous surface vessel encounters three fault events of different characters and the LLM produces reproducible operator-facing reports. A structured comparison against the two alternative reporting architectures available for this task, a rule-based template reporter driven by the same estimator and a flat-prompt LLM given the same numerical context, identifies open-ended query coverage at fixed numerical reliability as the property that neither alternative provides, and states the metrics under which that claim is to be tested.

This paper introduces Transdisciplinarity 3.x (TD 3.x) as an emerging next phase of transdisciplinary thought and practice for a complexity-saturated age. TD 3.x argues that complex problems require more than stakeholder inclusion, disciplinary boundary crossing, or procedural dialogue. They require stronger epistemic architecture, deeper reflexivity, greater realism about developmental unevenness, and a clearer understanding of adaptive challenges. The paper advances a metatheoretical approach grounded in the five dimensions of epistemology, ontology, axiology, praxis, and telos, while also incorporating a developmental lens, an adaptive leadership lens, and a model of hybrid human-AI cognition in which AI functions as part of an extended cognitive phenotype. It further links TD 3.x to the M3 Innovation Topology, showing how stronger epistemic design can support innovation across levels and loci. Finally, the paper proposes a multi-layered evaluative approach, combining rubrics with leading and lagging indicators to assess transdisciplinary quality and long-term developmental outcomes.

In this study, an artificial intelligence-assisted evaluation of the refractive indices of different materials is performed. The evaluation of the refractive index is necessary to design photonic devices for various classical and quantum photonic applications, and to theoretically analyse experimental results. The refractive index is one of the crucial parameters that affect the interaction of light with matter. Although the refractive index can be measured experimentally, its estimation via computational means provide the advantage of not requiring costly instrumentation, trained researchers and could avoid potential laboratory-based uncertainties. Therefore, in this study, artificial intelligence is implemented to estimate the optical constants of two types of materials, i.e., noble metals, and semiconductors. To this end, an artificial neural network is used to estimate the real and the imaginary parts of the refractive index of a specific material for various wavelengths of light. Then, the knowledge of the trained neural network is employed to initiate and train new neural networks to estimate the refractive indices of other materials. For the training of a neural network, various methods can be deployed. However, the application of the training can be a time-consuming process. A transfer learning approach is here implemented to provide a faster training solution for the problem under study. The implementation of transfer learning allows training the neural networks for a new material with higher speed or accuracy when compared to non-knowledge transfer-based training. Our results show the efficiency of the proposed technique in accurately evaluating the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index of different materials.

Abstract Canada’s emergency governance model no longer aligns with a risk environment shaped by accelerating climate change and increasingly complex multi-hazard events. Recent federal/provincial/territorial strategies acknowledge these growing pressures but have not materially reoriented federal leadership toward anticipatory risk governance, resulting in persistent gaps across jurisdictions. Using a conceptual analysis grounded in risk governance, resilience, and comparative federalism, this paper identifies four structural limitations that constrain national readiness: (1) fragmented situational awareness, (2) interoperability deficits, (3) a reactive federal posture, and (4) incomplete Indigenous integration. We propose a reshaped federal leadership model that operates continuously across the disaster cycle. The framework provides a concrete federal pathway linking governance theory to implementable design choices capable of strengthening national readiness and resilience in an era of compounding risk.

Objective: The primary goal of this study is to evaluate the transformative potential of integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Real-World Data (RWD) within global pharmacovigilance frameworks to automate adverse drug reaction detection, enhance regulatory decision-making efficiency, and establish a data-driven standard for precision medicine. To demonstrate how these innovations can align the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI) with international benchmarks like the FDA's Sentinel System to set a new global standard for drug safety surveillance. Key Findings: Incorporating Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning into high-speed data surveillance enables proactive signal detection using RWD from EHRs and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. Combining AI capabilities with trained human expertise accelerates drug safety workflows, optimizes clinical trial efficiency, and transforms proactive public health monitoring.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This working paper brings together draft recommendations developed by the five Task Forces of Thematic Working Group 6 (TWG6), “Women Shaping the AI Economy,” within the WIDCON project. It identifies policy and organisational actions to support women’s participation, quality employment and opportunities in an economy increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence. The document covers five interconnected areas: Evidence, monitoring and accountability. Regulatory scope and workforce impact governance. Good jobs, just transition and entrepreneurship. AI design and supply-side accountability. Structural barriers, skills and lifelong learning. A common framework connects the problems and available evidence to responsible actors, proposed actions, implementation routes, expected outcomes and monitoring signals. The document also records evidence limitations, external review status, illustrative practices and outstanding questions. Evidence strength and review maturity vary across the Task Force contributions. The working paper is prepared for discussion at the Dublin Summit, 15-16 October 2026, including the TWG6 session “AI for All and by All?”. It provides a basis for feedback from policymakers, employers, AI providers, social partners, researchers, education and training organisations, and civil society. This is an interim working paper for discussion. Summit feedback and subsequent review will inform further refinement of the recommendations. Final validation and formal adoption as a TWG6 position remain pending.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: AI-text detectors are already applied to Kazakh writing, yet no study reports how often publicly available detectors flag Kazakh text whose human authorship is dated before ChatGPT. We present AINA-KK: 3,811 human passages from encyclopedic, news, web and educational pages that provably existed before ChatGPT, and 5,597 machine and gray-zone passages from 9 generators, including the Kazakh-built KazLLM and Sherkala, with script and length stress tests. Five English-trained detectors from the Hugging Face Hub flag up to 81.4% of human passages and 79.6% of published student essays; recalibrated, they catch at most 1.3% of machine text. Calibrated zero-shot detectors catch at most 50.3% of machine text from in-distribution generators. Fine-tuned encoders rank text almost perfectly, but mDeBERTa at its default threshold flags 24.4% of 50-word human excerpts, partly because machine outputs are shorter than human text; calibrated, it catches only 47.1% of KazLLM and 62.7% of Sherkala passages. Without script handling, machine-transliterated Latin-2021 text defeats every detector. Fixes that need no new data (calibration, script canonicalization, script-augmented and length-matched training, and an OR with a zero-shot scorer) form AINA-KK-Det. On test it flags 0.9% of human passages (95% CI 0.4-2.7; 1.5% on development data) and catches 85.2% of machine text from known generators, 92.9% from two unseen Gemini-family Gemma-4 models and 61.3% from the Kazakh-built ones; its configuration was chosen with test results in view. We release the data, code and detector at https://github.com/ozxmn/aina-kk.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to digital art creation; however, its adoption in religious cultural heritage remains insufficiently understood because artistic production involves cultural symbolism, spiritual meaning, and human creativity. This study investigates artists’ perceptions of culturally sensitive AI adoption in Thai Buddhist digital art using survey data from 182 experienced digital Buddhist art designers in Thailand. An exploratory quantitative approach combining Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with Varimax rotation and multiple linear regression analysis was employed. PCA identified two empirically derived perceptual components: Perceived AI Capability and Perceived AI Benefits. Regression analysis revealed that Perceived AI Benefits was positively associated with artists’ evaluations of (a) Expectations for AI in Creating Buddhist Art, (b) Role of AI in Creating Buddhist Art, and (c) Technical Capability and Autonomous Functions of AI, whereas Perceived AI Capability was not significantly associated with any of these outcomes after controlling for perceived benefits. The findings indicate that perceived AI benefits are significantly associated with artists’ expectations and evaluations of AI in Thai Buddhist digital art. The findings also highlight broader considerations regarding cultural values, ethical responsibility, and human creative agency, providing a basis for human-centered and culturally sensitive AI applications in religious cultural heritage.

documents.abstract: Generative engines such as ChatGPT Web retrieve webpages to answer user queries, but only a subset are shown as citations. Understanding this retrieval-to-citation process is important for generative engine optimization (GEO), which aims to improve content visibility in generative-engine responses. However, prior studies mainly analyze final responses, leaving the internal execution process and its variation across model settings less understood. To this end, we conduct an observational study of four ChatGPT Web settings from ChatGPT 5.2 to 5.5, covering Instant and Thinking modes at the URL, hostname, and entity levels. We examine how ChatGPT rewrites queries, retrieves candidate webpages, and selects references. The Instant settings remain mostly single-round, while GPT-5.4 Thinking frequently performs multiple retrieval rounds. Across repeated runs, candidates retrieved more often are also more likely to be cited. We then evaluate Google Search and the OpenAI Responses API as external proxies. Responses API candidates provide broader coverage, while its citations more closely match sources cited by ChatGPT Web. Both proxies match ChatGPT Web better at the hostname and entity levels than at the exact-URL level. Even when combined, they recover only about one quarter of cited URLs. We further test whether these external signals remain predictive when combined. Within the external candidate set, a supervised model combining them reaches AUCs above 0.74 for GPT-5.3 and GPT-5.5 at all three levels. These findings suggest that GEO should distinguish retrieval visibility from citation visibility, account for rewritten queries and run-to-run variation, and consider hostname- and entity-level presence in addition to exact URLs. Differences across settings also suggest that GEO strategies should be re-evaluated when the deployed setting or serving environment changes.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and algorithmic task automation across modern enterprises has fundamentally accelerated skill obsolescence, creating an urgent strategic imperative for continuous employee upskilling and reskilling. This critical review systematically evaluates contemporary learning and development (L&D) strategies designed to foster workforce readiness in automated work environments. Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 systematic review protocol, a corpus of 16 peer-reviewed benchmark studies published between 2021 and 2026 was synthesized. The thematic analysis categorizes reskilling interventions into personalized AI-driven micro-learning, cross-functional hybrid technical-cognitive development, and human-agent cobot collaboration training. Meta-synthesized structural equation modeling indicates that structured reskilling initiatives exert a robust positive effect on workforce agility (β = .45, p < .001) mediated through skill self-efficacy and psychological job security. Furthermore, multi-level alignment—synchronizing national policy frameworks, organizational L&D infrastructure, and individual growth mindsets—emerges as a decisive boundary condition for sustainable employability. The paper concludes with an integrative governance framework guiding strategic HR leaders in mitigating automation-induced job displacement while enhancing organizational competitiveness.

Biogeochemical cycles occur naturally in coastal regions. Estuaries, wetlands, and tidal creeks assist these cycles. Since increased anthropogenic activities and naturally occurring events act as stressors, they impact physical, chemical, and biological processes in maritime spaces and hence these cycles. This makes existing ecosystems susceptible to trophic imbalance. Resultantly, researchers began monitoring and mapping coastal environments to understand how different stressors impact these biogeochemical processes using numerical and empirical models. With advances in computation infrastructure, use of data-driven techniques such as Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning in different hydrological systems have become commonplace. This has invigorated the use of predictive and decision-making frameworks in coastal management, making habitat conservation more scientific. Such frameworks balance ecological health and human activities through hard and soft engineering, nature-based solutions, and managed retreat. Though substantial literature on the use of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in the coastal environment exists, they focus on independent domains, with limited discussion of their combined impact on coastal management. Accordingly, this desk-based qualitative review discusses recent developments in Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and other data-driven techniques used for coastal management. Abstract Background. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are time-consuming, particularly at the study selection stage. Rayyan, a web and mobile AI-assisted screening platform, is widely used, including in francophone Africa, often without prior methodological training. Objective. To provide a didactic review of the use of Rayyan in conducting and reporting a systematic review with meta-analysis, in line with international recommendations on responsible AI use. Methods. Narrative synthesis of Rayyan's official documentation (accessed September 2026), studies describing and evaluating the tool, reporting guidelines (PRISMA 2020, PRISMA-S) and the 2025 joint position of Cochrane, the Campbell Collaboration, JBI and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence; illustration with an entirely fictitious worked example. Key messages. Rayyan supports reference import, deduplication, blinded multi-reviewer screening and conflict resolution and, depending on the plan, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and PRISMA flow diagrams. Its relevance ranking requires at least 50 decisions, including 5 inclusions and 5 exclusions. In one evaluation, sensitivity reached 97-99% at the most cautious threshold, with a specificity of only 19-58%. AI should therefore prioritise, not replace, human decisions, and its use must be reported. Conclusion. Used appropriately, Rayyan saves time and improves traceability; responsibility remains entirely human. Keywords: systematic review; meta-analysis; Rayyan; artificial intelligence; study selection; PRISMA 2020; sub-Saharan Africa.

documents.abstract: Global food security faces severe pressures from population growth, climate change and resource shortages. Traditional agricultural monitoring relies on manual sampling and offline laboratory testing, which involve considerable time delays and cannot realize continuous, in situ dynamic tracking of crop physiological status, field environment and agricultural product quality. Among the various sensing platforms for agriculture, flexible wearable sensors represent an important branch, featuring light weight, conformability, low power consumption and real-time response. It should be noted that rigid-substrate and silicon-based sensors remain indispensable in many agricultural applications, and this review focuses specifically on flexible wearable sensors while acknowledging the broader landscape of agricultural sensing technologies. Through conformal contact with plant surfaces or wearable integration, they can convert physical, chemical and biological signals of agroecosystems into readable electrical/optical signals via specific sensing transduction mechanisms. This review systematically categorizes wearable sensors for smart agriculture into two main types, optical and electrical, and elaborates their intrinsic sensing principles, summarizes typical application scenarios covering crop growth monitoring, post-harvest harvesting and agricultural product safety detection, and introduces the full-flow signal preprocessing, feature extraction and intelligent analysis technologies matched with wearable sensing data. Finally, the bottlenecks restricting large-scale field deployment of current wearable sensors are summarized, and the development directions of multi-modal integrated wearable sensing, biomimetic nanosensors inspired by natural plant sensing systems, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted agricultural monitoring platforms are prospected, aiming to provide a theoretical reference for the design optimization and popularization of agricultural wearable sensing equipment.
topics: Advanced Sensor and Energy Harvesting Materials

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has made verification a central educational concern. Current research increasingly asks whether students check AI-generated claims, how well they verify them, whether their trust is calibrated, and whether verification supports learning. A less developed question concerns the termination of verification: how does a learner decide that the available evidence is sufficient and that checking can reasonably stop? This conceptual article introduces Verification Sufficiency Calibration (VSC), defined as the degree to which a learner's decision to stop verifying a GenAI-supported claim is proportionate to the evidential demands, uncertainty, consequences, and disciplinary standards of the task. A targeted integrative review of recent research on GenAI literacy, verification behaviour, epistemic vigilance, evaluative judgement, trust calibration, and epistemic dependence was conducted through 3 October 2026. Recent work has documented task-sensitive verification thresholds and explicit 'enough checking' rules; it has distinguished verification initiation, quality, success, and reliance calibration; and it has developed broader AI-literacy and assessment-literacy measures. However, the adequacy of the stopping decision itself remains under-specified as a distinct educational construct. We propose a VSC framework that distinguishes under-verification, calibrated verification, and over-verification using task-specific acceptable evidence bands rather than a universal number of checks. Six propositions specify expected relations among VSC, task stakes, accountability, time pressure, prior knowledge, source cues, and transfer. We further propose a performance-based assessment architecture combining instrumented tasks, evidence-state scoring, stopping rationales, reliance decisions, and delayed AI-withdrawal transfer. VSC extends, rather than replaces, GenAI literacy, epistemic vigilance, evaluative judgement, and trust calibration by identifying an educationally consequential regulatory decision that lies between verification activity and subsequent reliance. The framework shifts responsible-AI education from the maxim 'always verify AI' towards a more demanding competence: knowing what requires verification, how much evidence is enough, and when continued checking no longer improves epistemic responsibility.

LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) use specialized agents that exchange messages to accomplish complex tasks. Their reliance on networked protocols, remote tools, and model endpoints exposes communication to message loss, delay, and context expiration. Because agents often exchange open-ended natural language, anomalies can alter task-relevant information while leaving messages processable, allowing semantic errors to propagate through subsequent interactions. Systematic studies of faults in inter-agent communication remain limited. This paper presents a large-scale empirical study of how communication faults manifest, propagate, and affect task outcomes in LLM-MAS. We construct a cross-layer taxonomy linking lower-stack disturbances to application-visible faults and develop a fault-injection and tracing pipeline. Our evaluation covers more than 29,000 executions across 100 tasks, five domains, three workflow topologies, and three model configurations. We find that 20.7% of failures with complete detection records occur without an immediate failure signal, reaching 76.2% for partial-content faults. Flat maintains 53.0% task success under communication faults, compared with 3.3% and 3.2% for Sequential and Hierarchical, respectively. This advantage primarily arises when an alternative information path preserves the evidence required by downstream agents. We also evaluate execution-side and evidence protection mechanisms and find that they recover different failure cases. Evidence recovery depends on whether trustworthy information remains accessible through an unaffected path. These observations provide empirical insights into communication-fault propagation, workflow resilience, and protection design for LLM-MAS.

Residential decarbonization increasingly relies on households to reduce electricity use and provide grid flexibility. These transitions can also create household benefits through lower electricity consumption. Yet households differ sharply in their ability to adopt the technologies that enable these outcomes. Housing tenure, financial resources, building age, and control over energy investments shape which technologies households can install and combine. Building on a previously developed agent-based model of residential technology adoption, we develop a sociotechnical modeling framework that traces how these structural conditions drive technology choices, reshape household technology portfolios, and alter time-resolved electricity demand. Applied to a synthetic population in the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power service territory, the model shows that structural constraints alter both the pace and composition of adoption. After ten simulated years, 70% of households in the least structurally constrained neighborhoods adopt at least three technologies, compared with 26% in the most structurally constrained neighborhoods. Earlier adoption and broader portfolios concentrate absolute annual electricity savings and peak-demand reductions in better-positioned neighborhoods. When annual savings are measured relative to baseline consumption, differences across groups largely narrow. By contrast, proportional peak-demand disparities persist because smart thermostats remain less common in more constrained neighborhoods. Unequal access to enabling technologies therefore shapes both the household benefits realized through demand-side decarbonization and the flexibility households can provide to the grid. These differences emerge before utility programs, incentives, or rate designs influence participation. Planning models that assume uniform household capabilities risk overstating the flexibility available from structurally constrained neighborhoods while concealing how demand-side benefits are unevenly distributed.

documents.abstract: Wildlife monitoring is essential for biodiversity conservation, ecological research, habitat management, and protection of endangered species. Traditional wildlife population monitoring methods often require extensive fieldwork, manual observation, and expert analysis, making them time-consuming and difficult to scale across large geographical regions. The development of computer vision, machine learning, and deep learning provides an opportunity to automate wildlife detection and population analysis using camera-trap images and videos. This paper presents a review of computer-vision-based approaches for zone-wise wildlife detection and population analysis. The proposed concept divides a wildlife reserve, forest, or protected area into geographical zones and uses camera traps or other imaging devices to collect data from each zone. Deep-learning models such as YOLO, Faster R-CNN, CNNs, ResNet, EfficientNet, Vision Transformers, and related object-detection techniques can be used to identify animal species and count detected individuals. The resulting information can be combined with the location of each camera to produce zone-wise species distributions, abundance estimates, and population trends. Recent research demonstratesthat automated wildlife detection can substantially reduce the manual effort required to process large camera-trap datasets. However, challenges remain in handling small and partially visible animals, different lighting conditions, dense vegetation, similar-looking species, class imbalance, changing habitats, and limited training data. Population estimation also requires consideration of imperfect detection and repeated observations. Future systems can combine computer vision, geographic information systems, edge AI, IoT sensors, and explainable artificial intelligence to provide real-time and zone-specific wildlife monitoring.

The increasing adoption of generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) in scientific writing has transformed scholarly communication while also raising concerns about authorship transparency and research integrity. The growing use of large language models (LLMs) has increased the need for methods that can screen AI-generated text while limiting false positives on human-written scientific prose. This study presents a lightweight hybrid framework that combines word-level TF–IDF features using 1–3-grams, character-level TF–IDF features using 3–6-grams, calibrated linear classification, and GPT-2-based language-model surprisal. The model outputs are combined through a weighted ensemble. Evaluation was conducted on a multi-corpus collection of 8,197 documents, comprising 4,100 human-written and 4,097 AI-generated documents, with a held-out evaluation set of 1,640 documents containing 820 documents from each class. The full ensemble achieved 95.80% accuracy, 97.10% precision, 94.35% recall, 95.71% F1-score, and 98.92% ROC-AUC. For the held-out human-written scientific documents, the reported specificity was 96.71%, corresponding to a false-positive rate of 3.29%. A separate five-fold stratified stability analysis on the complete corpus yielded a mean accuracy of 94.90% ± 0.53 and ROC-AUC of 98.58% ± 0.26. Within the evaluated corpus conditions, the findings demonstrate the potential of combining multi-granularity linguistic features and language-model surprisal for efficient scientific-text screening. The study provides a foundation for developing computationally efficient screening tools that can support editorial assessment, promote transparency in AI-assisted scientific writing, and contribute to research integrity while preserving human oversight.

Flight fatigue has been identified as a key factor contributing to human-factor-related safety incidents in civil aviation, significantly affecting pilots' cognitive and operational capabilities and posing a persistent threat to flight operational safety. However, the confined cockpit environment, together with vibration, electromagnetic interference, and other distinctive physical conditions, imposes substantial technical constraints on the real-time, continuous, and non-intrusive collection of fatigue data. Existing data acquisition methods differ considerably in sensor types, measurement indicators, and evaluation criteria, and the overall body of research remains fragmented, lacking a systematic review from the perspective of applicability in aeronautical engineering. This study first employs literature review and analytical methods to systematically categorize approaches to collecting crew fatigue data in civil aircraft cockpits across four dimensions: technical principles, application scenarios, acquisition requirements, and outcome evaluation. Second, a synthesis of empirical data reported in existing studies indicates that multimodal data fusion yields a substantially lower false-classification rate than single-indicator approaches and therefore offers greater value for early warning. Future research should focus on strengthening hardware interference-resistance design, developing localized real-time processing algorithms, and promoting unified industry standards for data collection and evaluation, thereby providing a feasible pathway for the intelligent advancement of flight safety management.

Background: Healthcare software built on the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standard now mediates prescribing, care coordination, and patient access at national scale, yet the quality assurance practices applied to such systems remain largely undifferentiated: a defect in a practitioner-directory lookup receives the same testing attention as a defect in a medication-dispensing workflow. Objective: This paper proposes a risk-based quality assurance framework for FHIR-based clinical applications that allocates verification effort in proportion to clinical consequence. Methods: The framework was constructed through a design-science methodology from three inputs: a case series of production failure modes documented on a HIPAA-regulated telehealth platform; quantified harm evidence from federal patient-safety research, including the finding that computerized provider order entry system-related errors occur in 0.3% to 6.3% of all prescriptions; and risk-management logic adapted from ISO 14971 and healthcare failure mode and effect analysis. The framework’s behavioral layer was then exercised against four FHIR server implementations using an open-source probe as one example realization. Results: The resulting model classifies FHIR resources and workflows into four risk tiers along three dimensions — clinical consequence class, data-integrity criticality, and failure detectability — and maps each tier to specific verification obligations spanning resource validation, workflow testing, and operational behavior probing. An assistive artificial-intelligence layer for preliminary risk classification is specified with a mandatory human validation gate. Illustrative application demonstrated that the highest-risk behavior identified by the framework — silent data-completeness failure in paginated synchronization — was present on one of the four tested servers while remaining invisible to profile validation and certification testing; the same exercise surfaced a previously undocumented rate-limiting defect, which was reported upstream. Conclusions: Verification effort for FHIR-based clinical systems can be allocated by clinical consequence rather than by test-suite convention, extending quality obligations into the operational-behavior layer where specification-conformant systems have been shown to fail. Empirical calibration across sites and defect corpora is the necessary next step, and the instrumentation for it is openly available.

To operate distributed applications with high availability, operators must rapidly diagnose and mitigate any incident. LLM-based agents can help, but unlike experienced human operators they do not improve as they handle more incidents. Each investigation starts from scratch, re-deriving likely causes and re-testing hypotheses even when a similar fault was resolved in the past. We present a self-defining operator (SDO) that improves with time by updating its operational behavior and memory. When SDO resolves an incident, it distills that experience into playbooks, which describe reusable diagnostic instructions for future incidents with similar faults, and detectors, scripts that take application telemetry as input and output relevant playbook(s). SDO continuously runs the detectors and invokes LLMs only when one fires, so its token cost scales with incident count rather than with operational time. Across 11 open-source microservice applications, SDO cuts resolution time by 52% on recurring faults while keeping per-incident cost low. SDO is open source at https://github.com/uw-syfi/sdo.

Promotional language in scientific and institutional documents is usually dismissed as individual failing or passing fashion. Using Bourdieu's field theory, the Sociology of Expectations and Bacchi's problem representation, we argue instead that it reflects scientific documents' structural position and institutional documents' functional mandate in governance. First, an expert-calibrated Large Language Model scores eight promotional dimensions across 268 natural hydrogen documents (1987-mid-2025). Hype, defined as evidential disproportion rather than forward-looking language, occupies the top two of five levels, whereas the models cover the full scale. Two metrics computed on each document's references translate Bourdieu's field theory into network terms, and both behave as it expects. Low out-closeness centrality, the strongest correlate, places those references at the margins of the field. A high hub score shows reliance on canonical authorities, whose symbolic capital the document borrows. Others are high novelty, absent direct measurements, hydrocarbon-system analogies, lower-prestige journals and a techno-economic or environmental focus, together explaining a third of the variance. The register rises as newcomers enter peripheral positions. Second, discourse analysis of 22 institutional documents (2021–2026) shows that register follows mandate. Enactors amplify expectations and Selectors temper them, as in the Sociology of Expectations. Hybrids, the role added here, write expectations into legal categories, funding calls and research agendas with a moderate register. Written into rules, unverified expectations act through procedure, not persuasion. Amplifying texts recur and push caveats to the margins, while tempering texts appear once. This imbalance in information, a constitutive element of procedural energy justice, precedes any participatory process.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied to an expanding range of scientific activities, including literature analysis, hypothesis generation, software development and automated experimentation. Yet these capabilities rely on a more fundamental condition: scientific information must remain identifiable and traceable across systems and over time. In practice, different versions of a work and their associated records and files are often scattered across services and local directories. This fragmentation forces researchers to identify and contextualize the same work repeatedly, disrupting continuity from discovery to interpretation and reuse. Here we present Gewu Insight, a research information infrastructure that addresses this discontinuity by organizing scientific works as persistent, stateful research objects. It unifies venue-, topic- and author-based discovery records through a shared paper identity. Within a local library, metadata, versioned resources and research context can then accumulate around the same work. These capabilities are integrated into an iterative workflow for scientist-led, AI-assisted research, allowing earlier interpretations to be revisited and refined. A bounded evaluation showed high candidate precision across the three discovery modes, with paper identity, resource distinctions and research state preserved in controlled workflows. By making continuity an explicit property of research infrastructure, Gewu Insight can serve as an inspectable scientific memory layer shared by researchers and AI assistants, supporting human judgment and providing a foundation for future, more epistemically grounded scientific AI.

Abstract Over-the-top (OTT) streaming platforms have moved beyond using artificial intelligence (AI) purely for content recommendation and are increasingly deploying it to set and personalise the price a subscriber sees. This study examines consumer awareness, comfort, and fairness perceptions surrounding AI-driven pricing on OTT platforms through a structured survey of 70 valid respondents, supported by a review of existing academic literature and a real-world industry case study. The research finds that awareness of algorithmic pricing is only moderate while fairness concern is strong: 52.9% of respondents said they were aware that OTT platforms use algorithms to personalise price, only 38.6% said they were comfortable paying a different price than another user for the same plan, and 61.4% said it would feel unfair if a friend paid less for an identical plan a gap of nearly 23 points between discomfort and perceived unfairness. When directly offered a choice between a plainly stated fixed price and a cheaper AI-personalised price, 51.4% of respondents chose the fixed price over the AI-personalised alternative, indicating that transparency outweighs the promise of a discount. Price transparency emerged as the single most valued factor in a subscription decision (34.3%), ahead of content library size, ad-free experience, personalised recommendations, and multi-profile sharing. A supporting case study of Netflix's password-sharing crackdown and ad-supported tier rollout illustrates that a well-executed, AI-enabled monetisation strategy can still deliver substantial subscriber and revenue growth even amid visible consumer frustration. The study concludes that AI-driven pricing is not a purely technical back-end function but a measurable driver of consumer trust, and that long-term commercial success depends on pairing algorithmic sophistication with genuine transparency toward the consumer. Keywords: AI-Driven Pricing, OTT Platforms, Dynamic Pricing, Consumer Behaviour, Price Fairness, Personalisation, Subscription Economy.

The growing pile of plastic waste has led to the implementation of sustainable engineering solutions, such as putting recycled plastics into asphalt mixtures, referred to as Plastic Waste-Modified Asphalt (PWMA). Despite the fact that in earlier studies, a significant improvement in mechanical performance, particularly stiffness and rutting resistance, has been demonstrated, there has been no emphasis on the environmental consequences related to it, particularly microplastic release (MPs). In line with this, Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models have been highly used in estimating the performance of pavement with a high level of accuracy, but their non-conventional characteristics make them hard to implement in the engineering profession. It is a systematic literature review that is based on PRISMA 2020 and aims to summarize the most up-to-date state-of-the-art in the crossroads of PWMA, advanced computational modeling, and environmental sustainability. 36 peer-reviewed articles that were published in 2019-2026 were examined. The results indicate that the DL models (particularly Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Neural Architecture Search-based models) have high predictive accuracy (R2 > 0.95), which is higher than the traditional ML methods. However, 32 of the 36 reviewed studies (88.9%) primarily focused on mechanical performance, whereas only 4 studies (11.1%) addressed microplastic-related environmental issues. In addition, there is an explainability gap, with only 4 of the 36 studies (11.1%) incorporating Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods. A suspected trade-off that is of critical importance in this paper is the possibility of a higher content of plastics to result in a higher stiffness but potentially higher rates of microplastic formation due to the brittle nature of materials. To overcome these shortcomings, a new Explainable Deep Learning (XDL) architecture is suggested that allows predicting mechanical performance and microplastic emissions simultaneously with greater interpretability. The specified strategy will be used to develop data-driven, transparent, and sustainable pavement design strategies.

Digitalization has been increasingly portrayed as a game-changing approach to enhancing construction safety through the adoption of technologies like Building Information Modelling (BIM), sensors, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and data analytics-based safety tools. While research interest and adoption of digital safety technologies have been increasing, the evidence of long-term improvement in safety performance is unclear. To understand this challenge, this research adopts a systematic review approach to critically synthesize the existing research on digitalization for construction safety, using the Theory-Context-Characteristics-Methodology (TCCM) framework. The review examined 120 peer-reviewed journal articles published from 2010 to 2026 to map research patterns, structural gaps, and cross-dimensional gaps. The results show a heavy emphasis on adoption-focused theories, location of studies in developed countries with little discussion of how they apply to developing construction settings, isolated technology-driven studies, and use of cross-sectional and perception-based research designs. These characteristics fuel a gap between digital technology adoption and safety outcomes. Drawing on the synthesis, this study develops the Digital Safety Readiness-Adoption-Outcome (DSRAO) framework, which conceptualizes digitalization in construction safety as a mediated and outcome-focused process. It places the organizational digital safety readiness as a key explanatory factor connecting contextual enablers and barriers, digital technology adoption, and explicit safety outcomes. The research contributes to the body of literature on digital construction safety by moving beyond descriptive synthesis and adoption-focused explanations, and providing an evidence-based and structured framework that explains how digitalization can enhance construction safety outcomes.

Electronic waste (e-waste) is a rapidly expanding environmental, economic and public-health challenge. Effective management requires more than legislation and physical recycling infrastructure; it also depends on the knowledge, attitudes, skills and participation of households, informal collectors, repairers, traders, community leaders, educators and producers. This paper examines the relationship between adult and non-formal education and e-waste policy and management, with particular attention to Nigeria. The paper adopts a qualitative documentary review approach, drawing on international reports, Nigerian environmental regulations, policy documents and relevant scholarly literature. The review indicates that adult and non-formal education can strengthen e-waste governance by translating technical regulations into locally understandable practices; developing occupational safety competencies among informal-sector actors; promoting repair, reuse, segregation, collection and responsible disposal; improving community participation; and creating pathways for green livelihoods. Nigeria has established an important regulatory foundation, including the National Environmental (Electrical/Electronic Sector) Regulations, 2022 and an extended producer responsibility approach, but persistent challenges include limited formal collection, inadequate recycling infrastructure, weak traceability, informal processing and gaps in awareness and enforcement. The paper proposes an integrated Adult and Non-Formal E-Waste Education Framework built around policy literacy, environmental literacy, occupational health and safety, technical skills, entrepreneurship, community mobilization, digital learning and monitoring. It concludes that adult and non-formal education should be treated as a core implementation instrument within e-waste policy rather than as an auxiliary awareness activity. Such an approach can support circular-economy transitions while improving livelihoods and reducing environmental and health risks.

Abstract Farmers frequently make decisions under uncertain weather, incomplete agricultural information, changing soil conditions, and limited access to timely expert guidance. The Agriculture and Farmer Digital Assistant (AFDA) is a web-based digital decision-support platform designed to bring agricultural data, artificial intelligence, recommendation services, weather information, and role-based administration into a single system. The platform accepts agricultural inputs from farmers and processes them to provide crop recommendations and basic farming guidance. The design also considers soil analysis, pest and disease support, market information, notifications, multilingual assistance, and future sensor integration. The implemented project version focuses on user registration and login, agricultural data input, crop recommendation, basic weather guidance, and a recommendation dashboard, while several advanced capabilities remain future extensions. A layered architecture separates the user interface, application logic, AI processing, database, and notification/recommendation functions. The project further defines functional and non-functional requirements, data-flow and entity relationships, user workflows, testing procedures, and maintenance considerations. The reported evaluation is functional rather than numerical: the major input, authentication, recommendation, navigation, and output-display workflows were checked during development, while no measured accuracy or response-time benchmark is claimed. AFDA therefore provides a foundation for a connected and extensible agricultural assistance system intended to support better-informed and more sustainable farming decisions. Keywords Agriculture and Farmer Digital Assistant, AFDA, artificial intelligence, machine learning, crop recommendation, smart farming, agricultural decision support, weather guidance, role-based access control.

INTRODUCTION: Large language models (LLMs) can enhance learning engagement and accessibility, though their performance in dentistry is inconsistent. Bitewing radiographs are critical for caries detection but prone to diagnostic errors from operator positioning. This study compared the performance of four LLMs with reasoning capabilities, GPT o1, GPT o3-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash and Grok 3, in generating scenario-specific educational feedback from a structured textual format of bitewing radiographs. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Ten positioning error scenarios were created by DMFR specialists. LLMs were evaluated using an original prompt (OP) and an engineered prompt (EP), resulting in a 4 × 2 LLM-by-prompt design. Each LLM was tested via its model-specific access mode: API or web interface. Eighty outputs were assessed by two DMFR specialists for detail, content, clarity and relevance using a 5-point Likert scale. Ordinal category-level scores were analysed using a cumulative link mixed-effects model, with LLM, prompt type, scenario group, assessment category and LLM × prompt as fixed effects, and scenario as a random intercept. RESULTS: The LLM-prompt interaction was significant, indicating prompt engineering affected models differently. GPT o3-mini had significantly lower odds of higher scores than Gemini 2.0 Flash, while EP reduced Grok 3 performance. Positioning error type influenced performance, with significant model-dependent differences across scenario groups. No significant LLM-assessment category interaction was observed, suggesting model differences did not vary across assessment categories. CONCLUSION: LLM-generated feedback varied by model, prompt design and positioning error type, but not consistently across assessment categories. Outputs require validation, model-specific prompt testing and specialist review before implementation.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background There are a growing number of cases where direct use of AI has been associated with either new or worsening psychiatric symptoms (colloquially labelled AI psychosis). Due to the novelty of the phenomenon, current literature is limited on the impacts of sustained, emotionally charged interactions with AI chatbots. This narrative review of publicly available reports and media accounts aims to address this gap by identifying reports of AI-associated psychiatric symptoms. Methods Given the novelty of the topic, reports published from inception to March 1, 2026, were identified from Google News and Google Scholar. Search terms included: “artificial intelligence,” “AI chatbot,” “ChatGPT,” “Character.AI,” and “large language model,” combined with terms such as “psychosis,” “delusion,” “depression,” “anxiety,” “suicide,” and “spiritual.” These terms were selected to focus on reports that describe psychiatric symptoms associated with AI use, while excluding general articles on AI ethics, technology, or public opinion. Two authors conducted an independent analysis of the results, and all authors reached a consensus on the publications to include in this review. While websites such as Reddit contain over 100 different threads of cases dealing with AI chatbot-associated psychiatric symptoms, they were excluded due to a lack of information. Results Nineteen cases were identified describing users who developed a sustained emotional reliance on AI chatbots. Across cases, this developed regardless of the original reason for chatbot use and was associated with the emergence of psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety, depressive symptoms, delusional beliefs, and suicidal ideation. In many cases where the user expressed suicidal ideation, chatbots responses reportedly lacked appropriate crisis intervention and, in some cases, reinforced the users’ beliefs. Conclusion AI chatbot-associated psychiatric symptoms are an emerging concern with new cases increasingly being reported. This review explores such cases while also serving as a call to action for more research and discussion on how to address the risks of AI use.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in modern business environments, fundamentally reshaping how organizations collect information, generate knowledge, make decisions, and create value. The convergence of AI and Business Intelligence (BI) enables enterprises to move beyond descriptive reporting toward predictive and prescriptive decision-making frameworks. Simultaneously, entrepreneurs and startups increasingly employ AI-powered analytics, intelligent automation, and machine learning to identify market opportunities, optimize operations, and develop innovative products and services. This article examines the evolving relationship between AI, Business Intelligence, and entrepreneurship, highlighting how organizations leverage data-driven intelligence for sustainable competitive advantage and organizational innovation. Drawing upon contemporary research and practical examples, the article explores technological foundations, leadership implications, entrepreneurial opportunities, global and local applications, and future challenges. The discussion emphasizes that successful adoption of AI requires not only technical capabilities but also strategic leadership, ethical governance, and a culture of continuous innovation.
